# Identity and access operations

This document is the operator contract for the approved identity and access boundary. Runtime
implementation must consume the typed values from `src/config/env.ts`; it must not duplicate or
silently override them.

## Security policy

- The web refresh credential uses the exact cookie name `__Host-wedding-refresh` with
  `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`, and no `Domain` attribute.
- Access credentials live for 10 minutes. Refresh sessions expire after 30 idle days or 90 days
  absolutely, whichever comes first. Password-reset credentials live for 30 minutes.
- Workspace invitations live for 72 hours. At most three issues or reissues are allowed for one
  consultation/email pair in 24 hours.
- Passwords contain 12–128 Unicode characters and at most 512 UTF-8 bytes. The approved scrypt
  parameters are `N=131072`, `r=8`, `p=1`, a 64-byte derived key, and 256 MiB `maxmem`.
- Opaque access, refresh, invitation, and reset credentials use 32 random bytes before base64url
  encoding. Only purpose-separated deterministic hashes may cross the credential boundary into
  persistence, logs, errors, or snapshots.
- Login and one-time-token consumption allow 10 attempts per 15 minutes. Reset requests allow
  three per hour. Refresh allows 60 per 15 minutes. These are separate fail-closed buckets; no
  permanent account lockout is allowed.
- Invitation, password-reset, and expired/revoked session records are retained for 180, 30, and
  90 days. Disabled-account PII becomes eligible for deletion after 365 days only when terminal
  linked-record facts permit it. Legal and financial holds take precedence.

Staging and production must explicitly set every `AUTH_*` value shown in `.env.example`. The
parser accepts only the approved values. Development and test receive the same policy defaults;
only trusted-proxy hops default to zero. Set `AUTH_TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=1` only when exactly one
controlled reverse proxy sits between the application and every client. Any other topology needs
a reviewed configuration change before deployment.

## Initial Manager bootstrap

Manager creation is an operator-only deployment operation. There is no public registration route
and no generic role-assignment endpoint.

The IA-04 bootstrap command must enforce this sequence:

1. An authorized operator opens an audited shell in the target deployment and confirms the exact
   database and environment.
2. The operator supplies the normalized Manager email and display data as command options. The
   password is read from an interactive hidden prompt or an approved secret-file descriptor—never
   from command-line arguments, logs, shell history, or a checked-in environment file.
3. The command starts one database transaction, refuses to run if any Manager role already exists,
   creates the account/password verifier/Manager role, and emits an audit record identifying the
   operator and deployment request.
4. The operator verifies a successful audit event, removes any one-time secret material, and closes
   the audited shell. Re-running the command must fail closed.

Routine Manager or Staff lifecycle changes must use explicit privileged workflows with audit
events. Customer invitation acceptance may add only the `COUPLE` role scoped through consultation
access and can never grant `MANAGER` or `STAFF`.

## Identity retention execution

The identity retention command is operator-only and has no HTTP route. It processes one bounded
batch, rechecks D6 eligibility in PostgreSQL, anonymizes due disabled-account PII, revokes remaining
authentication material, and deletes terminal invitation, password-reset, and session metadata
after 180, 30, and 90 days respectively.

Before every run, confirm `DATABASE_URL` names the intended database and, when applicable, schema.
Then run:

```powershell
npm run retention:identity -- --confirm-retention --batch-size=100
```

The command refuses to run without `--confirm-retention`, accepts only batch sizes from 1 to 1,000,
and emits counts without account identifiers, email addresses, or credentials. Re-run until all
counts are zero. The operation is idempotent and concurrent workers use PostgreSQL row locks with
`SKIP LOCKED`, so one account is anonymized at most once. Never point a development retention run
at the shared Supabase `public` schema.

An anonymized account retains its UUID only as a pseudonymous business/audit reference. Its login
and display emails move to the reserved `identity.invalid` domain, its password verifier is deleted,
active sessions and one-time credentials are revoked, invitation recipient email is scrubbed, and
`piiAnonymizedAt` records completion. Legal/financial holds and missing terminality facts fail
closed.

## Scrypt benchmark evidence

On 2026-10-03, the approved parameters were measured on the Windows development host under Node
24 with three sequential hashes: 388 ms, 346 ms, and 317 ms (350 ms mean). The configured `maxmem`
ceiling is 256 MiB and the scrypt working-set estimate is approximately 128 MiB per concurrent
hash. Deployment sizing must therefore bound concurrent password work and repeat this benchmark on
the production compute class before launch; changing the cost requires a reviewed policy revision
and causes successful verification of older records to request rehash.
````

# Brevo transactional email

The backend uses Brevo's HTTP API for password reset emails and the shared workspace invitation notification port. Startup does not send an email. A blank email configuration uses the offline fake in development/test; staging and production require real email configuration.

## Account setup

1. Register at [Brevo](https://www.brevo.com/) and complete the requested account checks. Ensure transactional email sending is enabled for the account.
2. Open **Settings > SMTP & API > API Keys & MCP** ([API keys](https://app.brevo.com/settings/keys/api)). Generate an API key named `wedding-be-local` and save it immediately. Use an **API key**, not an SMTP key or MCP-specific key. See [API key authentication](https://developers.brevo.com/docs/api-key-authentication).
3. Open **Settings > Senders, Domains, IPs > Senders**, then **Add a sender**. Enter the name `Wedding Restaurant` and an email address you control. If the domain is not authenticated, confirm the verification code sent to that mailbox. See [sender verification](https://help.brevo.com/hc/en-us/articles/208836149-Create-a-new-sender-From-name-and-From-email).
4. Without a custom domain, a verified free email address can be used during setup. Brevo replaces free sender addresses with an address under its own sending domain, including transactional messages; recipients may therefore see a different From address. Brevo describes this as a temporary measure and recommends an authenticated custom domain for long-term use. See [sender address replacement](https://help.brevo.com/hc/en-us/articles/14925263522578-Comply-with-Gmail-Yahoo-and-Microsoft-s-requirements-for-email-senders).

## Backend configuration

Edit `wedding-be/.env` locally; the following values are examples, not working credentials:

```dotenv
BREVO_API_KEY=replace-with-your-api-key
BREVO_FROM_EMAIL="Wedding Restaurant <your-project-email@gmail.com>"

RESEND_API_KEY=
RESEND_FROM_EMAIL=
```

The sender address must match the sender verified in Brevo. Both Brevo values must be supplied together. Only one provider may be configured at a time; clear both Resend values when using Brevo. All four values may be blank for offline development/test. Never put these credentials in frontend variables, `.env.example`, or Git.

Restart the backend after changing `.env`:

```powershell
npm run dev
```

## Check delivery

With PostgreSQL configured and an existing eligible account, request a password reset using the application's forgot-password flow. Inspect **Transactional > Email > Logs** in Brevo, and check the recipient's inbox and spam folder. Unknown accounts do not receive a reset email. A successful API response means Brevo accepted the message; final delivery is reported by Brevo's logs.

If sending fails, check the API key, verified sender, transactional account activation, remaining sending quota, and any IP authorization request from Brevo. The backend deliberately returns sanitized provider errors rather than exposing email addresses, reset links, raw provider messages, or keys.

## Adapter behavior

- Sends to `POST https://api.brevo.com/v3/smtp/email` using the `api-key` HTTP header, a parsed sender, recipients, subject, text, and optional HTML. See [API reference](https://developers.brevo.com/reference/sendtransacemail).
- Validates commands and response message IDs, rejects redirects, and aborts requests after 10 seconds, including response body reading. HTTP 429/5xx and transport errors map to provider unavailability; other rejected requests map to a generic provider error. There are no automatic retries.
- Converts the full persisted event/entity intent into a deterministic UUID v5 for Brevo's `headers.idempotencyKey`, preserving the same key across restarts and separating different intent types. Brevo documents a **30-minute** deduplication window and a `duplicate_parameter` rejection for reused keys. A rejected duplicate is a provider error, not a replay of the original success. This does not replace durable application delivery/audit state. See [Brevo idempotency](https://developers.brevo.com/docs/heterogenous-versions-batch-emails).
- Retains Resend for existing environments configured with only `RESEND_API_KEY` and `RESEND_FROM_EMAIL`.

Tests use controlled HTTP doubles; they do not send real email:

```powershell
npm test -- src/integrations/email src/config/env.test.ts
```
````

# Dependency audit gate

CI runs `npm run audit:ci`, which executes npm's lockfile-based audit at the
`high` threshold. The gate fails closed when npm returns malformed data, when a
new high/critical advisory is not documented, or when a matching exception has
reached its `reviewBy` date.

Temporary exceptions live in `dependency-audit-exceptions.json`. Each entry
records the advisory identity, affected package, reachability, mitigation,
owner, and mandatory review date. An exception does not change package
resolution and is not a general severity waiver. Remove it as soon as the
committed dependency graph no longer reports the advisory.

Do not use `npm audit fix --force`: it may cross the approved Prisma dependency
line. Review a compatible upstream release, update the exact pins and lockfile,
then run the complete quality and PostgreSQL integration gates before removing
an exception.
```

# ADR-001: Model Revised Wedding Operations with Existing Capabilities

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-09-26

## Context

The approved product direction adds five connected changes:

- timeline collaboration must happen before deposit;
- wedding photos are shared with the restaurant only after deposit;
- the seating plan selects a restaurant layout and labels tables by guest group instead of assigning people to seats;
- staff check in invitation households by name and actual arrival count instead of relying on per-recipient QR codes;
- physical invitation printing supports multiple variants and quantities, uses a generic public QR, and contributes accepted charges to booking receivables.

The existing capability map already defines stable module IDs and a 10-week academic delivery boundary. The decision must preserve an acyclic dependency graph, backend-authoritative rules, and practical scope.

## Decision

Keep the existing module IDs and allocate the revised behavior as follows:

- `identity-access` owns restricted prospect access and promotion of the same identity to full Couple access.
- `venue-catalog` owns reusable timeline templates and immutable seating-layout templates with supported capacity ranges.
- `booking-lifecycle` owns consultation workspaces, timeline revisions and approvals, deposit eligibility, and post-deposit timeline change requests.
- `payments-billing` owns accepted print charges and receivables.
- `invitation-studio` owns the post-deposit media library, generic public invitation QR, printable snapshots, and print-order fulfillment.
- `guest-rsvp` owns invitation households and guest-group definitions.
- `seating-plan` consumes layout templates and guest groups to label fixed tables.
- `staff-operations` owns manual multi-arrival check-in and audited attendance correction.
- `notifications-automation` and `analytics-dashboard` consume the resulting events and read models.

`invitation-studio` now depends on `payments-billing`; therefore the two capabilities are no longer approved as parallel top-level modules. Guest groups remain owned by `guest-rsvp` so seating can depend on them without creating a guest/seating dependency cycle.

The pre-deposit experience uses an authenticated restricted Web workspace. The physical-invitation QR is generic and public; it is not guest identity, RSVP authorization, or a check-in credential.

## Alternatives Considered

### Create New `event-planning`, `media-library`, and `print-fulfillment` Modules

- Pros: Narrower modules and clearer names for each new capability.
- Cons: More contracts, specifications, implementation checkpoints, and coordination within the fixed delivery window.
- Rejected: The behaviors fit existing ownership without cycles, and adding three modules would increase delivery risk more than it would improve separation.

### Grant Full Couple Access Before Deposit

- Pros: One permission set and fewer visible account states.
- Cons: Unconfirmed prospects would mix with paying customers and gain access to guest, media, invitation, seating, and print workflows too early.
- Rejected: A restricted workspace matches the sales process and preserves a clear commercial boundary.

### Use a Long-Lived Public Consultation Link

- Pros: Lowest sign-in friction.
- Cons: Forwarded links could expose proposals or permit unauthorized timeline edits; revocation and actor attribution would be weak.
- Rejected: An expiring bootstrap invitation followed by an authenticated session provides traceability without requiring a separate account after deposit.

### Keep Per-Guest Table Assignment and QR Check-In

- Pros: More precise seating and faster check-in when complete guest data exists.
- Cons: Requires detailed guest data, many physical QR codes, more correction work, and operational behavior that does not match the restaurant's area-guidance process.
- Rejected: Invitation-household check-in and guest-group table labels are more realistic and require less personal data.

### Let Print Orders Reference Live Invitation Data

- Pros: No snapshot model.
- Cons: A later timeline, seating, design, or price edit could silently change what an approved order is expected to print.
- Rejected: Approval must freeze printable and commercial revisions for auditability and reprint accuracy.

## Consequences

- The approved module IDs and repository topology remain unchanged.
- The dependency order becomes more sequential because invitation printing consumes billing.
- Backend authorization must distinguish restricted Prospect and full Couple capabilities without duplicating identities.
- Timeline and print approvals require immutable revision identities.
- Guest-group identifiers become a shared contract used by guests, seating, staff operations, and analytics.
- Exact guest seating, table-geometry editing, printed recipient names, per-recipient physical QR codes, and QR check-in are not required capabilities.
- Module specs must trace to `PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md` and may refine deferred numeric limits without changing this decision.
```

# ADR-002: Freeze Program Contracts Before Parallel Specification

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-10-06

## Context

The original program plan requires each module specification, implementation, evidence,
and owner approval to finish before the next dependent specification begins. That
sequence protects unresolved contracts but prevents new contributors from owning later
specifications concurrently.

The project owner wants to define and reconcile the cross-module contract baseline for
all remaining capabilities first. Once ownership, state semantics, provider ports,
events, snapshots, and compatibility rules agree, separate contributors should be able
to specify and plan different modules without creating conflicting domain models.

The repository already has implemented contracts for `core-platform` and
`identity-access`, approved contracts for `venue-catalog`, stable module IDs, and an
acyclic capability map. The remaining risk is not the absence of module boundaries; it
is allowing separate specifications to silently redefine the same boundary.

`SPEC-02` is already being implemented under an approved venue-catalog plan. Reopening
or replanning that work would add risk without helping the remaining contract freeze.

## Decision

Adopt `CONTRACT-BASELINE.md` as the single versioned cross-module contract for the
Wedding Management program.

Under the project-owner-approved version `1.0.0`:

- `SPEC-02` continues unchanged through its existing V4 acceptance gate;
- contributors may draft `SPEC-03` through `SPEC-11` with controlled overlap, while
  final provider/consumer contract approvals remain dependency-ordered and each
  module plan still waits for approval of its own SPEC;
- each SPEC must declare the baseline version it consumes and list its produced and
  consumed provider contracts/events;
- one provider module owns each identifier, fact, state transition, and event schema;
- consumer SPECs may refine local behavior but cannot fork or override provider
  semantics;
- incompatible discoveries use the baseline change procedure rather than silent edits;
- implementation follows dependency readiness, a serialized migration lane, and real
  provider integration gates even when specifications were written in parallel.

The required final SPEC approval graph is `03 → 04 → 05 → 06`, followed by
`07 → 08 → 10` in parallel with `09`; `11` waits for both `09` and `10`. Early
drafting does not waive these gates.

The contract baseline does not create a shared runtime package. Backend interfaces
remain in their owning modules, and client types remain generated from the backend
OpenAPI artifact.

## Alternatives Considered

### Keep the Fully Sequential Specification Sequence

- Pros: Every downstream author sees a completed upstream implementation.
- Cons: New contributors remain idle or work without ownership; feedback on later
  cross-module assumptions arrives late.
- Rejected if the baseline is accepted: Contract review can resolve semantic
  dependencies before implementation without serializing all documentation work.

### Start Every Module Implementation in Parallel

- Pros: Maximum apparent concurrency.
- Cons: Shared Prisma migrations, money/access effects, provider availability, and
  end-to-end invariants still have real order; mocks can hide incompatible behavior.
- Rejected: Parallel specification does not eliminate implementation dependencies.

### Create a Shared Cross-Repository Types Package

- Pros: One importable location for interfaces.
- Cons: Creates a fifth artifact, duplicates OpenAPI distribution, couples client and
  backend release cadence, and risks leaking internal domain types.
- Rejected: The baseline documents semantics, owner modules publish backend ports, and
  OpenAPI remains the external client contract.

### Let Each SPEC Negotiate Contracts Independently

- Pros: Minimal up-front coordination.
- Cons: Encourages duplicate ownership, incompatible enums, reversed dependencies,
  and late integration rework.
- Rejected: It does not satisfy the reason for parallel specification.

## Consequences

- Cross-module decisions receive earlier review and become explicit versioned
  commitments.
- Multiple contributors can own separate SPECs and plans after one baseline approval.
- SPEC-02 continues without baseline-driven replanning, and SPEC-03 implementation
  remains blocked until venue-catalog V4 acceptance.
- Contract changes become more deliberate and require impact analysis.
- Some detailed module choices remain intentionally deferred; the baseline must not
  grow into a monolithic implementation specification.
- Provider implementations, migrations, money effects, and final integration still
  respect dependency order and acceptance gates.
- The capability map and task plan record the accepted dependency graph and controlled
  overlap rules from the baseline lock.

## Approval Record

The project owner accepted this decision and locked
`WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.0.0` on 2026-10-06. Future changes follow the baseline's
compatibility and change-control procedure; this ADR remains as the historical record
of why controlled parallel specification was introduced.
```

# ADR-003: Publish Provider Hand-offs for Overlapping Implementation

## Status

Accepted by the project owner on 2026-10-06. Supplements accepted ADR-002 without
replacing its module-plan, implementation and acceptance gates.

## Context

The owner clarified that independent team implementation means different contributors
can implement SPEC slices concurrently where dependencies permit. The first drafts
restated semantic boundaries but lacked ordered source evidence, snapshot/search ports,
billing adjustments, automation commands and explicit implementation readiness.

## Decision

Adopt accepted WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0 Section 21 and the revised SPEC-03 through
SPEC-11. Separate approved contracts, isolated coding with conforming fakes, specific
real provider readiness, consumer integration, and whole-module acceptance.

An approved module/plan can implement against a reviewed provider contract while that
provider's implementation is unfinished. Specific real methods may become ready before
all upstream screens finish. Deposit, access, print snapshot and attendance acceptance
requires real providers and PostgreSQL. The principal integration spine and the
seating/staff/analytics versus notification branches remain.

One steward serializes core outbox/unit-of-work, additive identity/venue prerequisites,
Prisma migrations, OpenAPI publication and composition-root wiring. Module owners
implement their own application ports and files. Existing 1.0.0 signatures remain;
new ports provide ordered headcount, reporting, search and automation.

## Alternatives

- Whole-program sequential coding prevents useful overlap after interfaces stabilize.
- Simultaneous all-module integration ignores money/history/migration dependencies.
- Consumer repository reads bypass ownership and make independent testing unreliable.

## Consequences

Each SPEC has DTOs, defaults, failures, provider/fake proof and parallel-work matrices.
Integration/acceptance remain ordered; shared-file changes have one lane. Numeric
policies are fixed by this SPEC approval. Existing CP/IA/VC acceptance stays intact.
The initial three-person allocation is A: SPEC-03/04, B: SPEC-05/06 and C: SPEC-07/08.
SPEC-09/10/11 and the named integration steward are not yet assigned.

## Approval

Approval evidence (2026-10-06): the project owner replied, “vậy tôi duyệt draft trên”,
after reviewing the revised SPEC-03 through SPEC-11, hand-off dependencies and the
three-person ownership split. Contract revision 1.1.0 and the nine specifications are
approved together. This does not approve unprepared module task/wave plans, mark any
provider as implemented, accept a module, or authorize deployment.

References: [accepted amendment 1.1.0](../../CONTRACT-BASELINE.md#21-accepted-amendment-110-implementation-hand-off-contracts),
[team implementation](../team-implementation.md), and [ADR-002](0002-freeze-program-contracts-before-parallel-specification.md).
```

# Implementation Plan: Wedding Management System

Core-platform plan status: Approved by project owner on 2026-09-24<br>
Post-core program extension status: Approved by project owner on 2026-09-27<br>
Cross-module contract baseline: Locked as
[`WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0`](../CONTRACT-BASELINE.md) on 2026-10-06 (1.0.0 history retained)<br>
SPEC-03 through SPEC-11 and three-person ownership: Approved on 2026-10-06;<br>
bounded module task/wave plans and implementation acceptance remain pending.<br>
Approved platform specification: [`../SPEC-core-platform.md`](../SPEC-core-platform.md)<br>
Approved product requirements: [`../PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md`](../PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md)<br>
Capability map: [`../CAPABILITY-MAP.md`](../CAPABILITY-MAP.md)<br>
Task list: [`todo.md`](./todo.md)<br>
Initially prepared: 2026-09-24<br>
Extended: 2026-09-27

## 1. Overview

Implement the approved wedding-management capabilities across four independent repositories in the dependency order recorded by `CAPABILITY-MAP.md`. The currently detailed CP-01 through CP-32 work establishes `core-platform`: reproducible TypeScript toolchains, a production-minded Express/Prisma foundation, a generated OpenAPI contract, three typed API clients, provider boundaries, security/observability primitives, and independent CI quality gates.

The post-core extension adds rolling specification and planning gates for every later
module. `WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0` permits controlled overlap after contract approval.
SPEC-03 through SPEC-11 are now approved, but a module receives executable implementation
tasks only after its bounded plan is prepared and approved. This preserves completed and
in-progress history while preventing unapproved API, state-machine, security, or
data-retention assumptions from entering implementation tasks.

The plan remains front-loaded with the highest-risk foundations: PostgreSQL migration behavior, HTTP/error conventions, idempotency concurrency, deterministic API generation, prospect-to-Couple authorization, revision-bound approvals, private media, attendance concurrency, and immutable print snapshots.

## 2. Planning Assumptions

- At the initial plan approval all four repositories were empty. CP-01 through CP-06 are now complete; CP-07 onward remain governed by their existing checklist state in `todo.md`.
- `wedding-be/tasks/` is the coordination location for this cross-repository capability. Product code remains in its owning repository.
- Implementation uses a short-lived `codex/core-platform` branch in each repository unless the project owner requests direct work on the saved checkout.
- Each repository owns its own npm manifest, lockfile, CI workflow, and commit history.
- The implementation may use fake providers for all automated tests; live Supabase, Resend, Gemini, and EAS credentials are not required to complete local foundation tasks.
- Framework-generated scaffold files are reviewed as one scaffold operation, but human-authored follow-up tasks remain limited to approximately five files.
- Phase estimates are sequencing guidance, not delivery promises; verification evidence determines completion.
- `PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md` and the revised capability map are approved, but no later module is authorized for implementation until its module specification and detailed task slice pass their own human review gate.
- The task list is a rolling plan: completed CP tasks are immutable history, unchecked CP tasks remain active, and later module tasks are inserted only by the corresponding specification gate.
- `SPEC-02` remains governed by its approved venue-catalog plan through V4. The
  baseline does not reopen it, and no `booking-lifecycle` implementation starts before
  V4 acceptance.
- Every SPEC from `SPEC-03` onward declares
  `contractBaseline: WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0`, retains inherited 1.0.0 history and lists its produced and consumed
  provider contracts and events.

## 3. Architecture Decisions Carried into Implementation

1. `wedding-be` is the only database and business-rule authority.
2. All repositories use Node.js 24 LTS, npm, strict TypeScript, ESLint flat config, Prettier, and committed lockfiles.
3. Zod request/response schemas in the backend generate OpenAPI 3.1; client repositories consume the artifact through generated types and one `openapi-fetch` wrapper.
4. Prisma migrations are the only shared-environment schema-change mechanism. Integration tests use real PostgreSQL semantics.
5. Audit records and idempotency records are infrastructure primitives; no wedding-domain tables are introduced.
6. Supabase Storage, Resend, and Gemini SDKs remain behind local provider interfaces with fake adapters.
7. Logs are operational telemetry; PostgreSQL audit records are durable evidence. The two are never substituted for one another.
8. CI is independent per repository. A client CI job verifies an OpenAPI artifact from an immutable backend commit/release, not a moving branch.
9. Android is the only mobile acceptance target. `core-platform` validates configuration and Expo health; `release-demo` owns the final EAS artifact.
10. A prospective couple uses authenticated restricted Web access before deposit; a successful deposit promotes the same identity to full Couple access.
11. Timeline and print approvals bind to immutable revisions, and deposit eligibility is rechecked authoritatively by the backend.
12. Guest groups belong to `guest-rsvp`; fixed layout geometry belongs to `venue-catalog`; table labeling belongs to `seating-plan`.
13. Event check-in records invitation-household arrivals and corrections rather than per-seat occupancy or physical-invitation QR credentials.
14. `payments-billing` precedes `invitation-studio` because accepted print charges become booking receivables.
15. Cross-module ownership, identifiers, events, snapshot semantics, compatibility,
    and change control are fixed by active `WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0`; conflicting module
    choices require a baseline change proposal first.

## 4. Dependency Graph

```text
Approved spec and capability map
           │
           ├───────────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────┐
           ▼               ▼                ▼                 ▼
   Backend toolchain   Public Web       Manage Web        Expo App
           │            foundation       foundation        foundation
           ▼               │                │                 │
   Backend lifecycle       │                │                 │
           │               │                │                 │
     HTTP contracts        │                │                 │
       ┌───┴─────┐         │                │                 │
       ▼         ▼         │                │                 │
  Prisma core  OpenAPI ────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┘
       │         │         ▼                ▼                 ▼
       │         │   Public client     Manage client      App client
       │         │
       ├─────────┼──────► Audit / idempotency
       │         │
       └─────────┴──────► Security / observability
                         │
                         ├────────► Storage adapter
                         ├────────► Email adapter
                         └────────► AI image adapter

All verified slices ──────────────► Per-repository CI ──► Acceptance audit
```

## 5. Delivery Strategy

### Phase A — Reproducible repository foundations

Goal: every repository can install, lint, typecheck, test, and build before cross-repository integration begins.

Tasks:

- CP-01 Backend package and compiler baseline.
- CP-02 Backend lint, formatting, and test harness.
- CP-03 Public Web package and Next.js configuration.
- CP-04 Public Web application shell and smoke test.
- CP-05 Management Web package and Next.js configuration.
- CP-06 Management Web application shell and smoke test.
- CP-07 Expo package and SDK-compatible configuration.
- CP-08 Expo Router shell and Android smoke test.

Parallelization:

- CP-01/02, CP-03/04, CP-05/06, and CP-07/08 are four independent repository streams.
- Within each stream, configuration precedes the application shell.

Checkpoint A:

- Clean `npm ci` succeeds in every repository.
- Lint, typecheck, unit-test, and build scripts exist and pass.
- Expo additionally passes `npx expo-doctor`.

### Phase B — Backend process and HTTP contract

Goal: provide a testable Express process with validated configuration and stable HTTP semantics before persistence or integrations are attached.

Tasks:

- CP-09 Backend environment/configuration boundary.
- CP-10 Express composition and graceful process lifecycle.
- CP-11 Request context, standard errors, and Zod validation.
- CP-12 Health and readiness vertical slice.

Order:

- CP-09 precedes CP-10.
- CP-11 depends on the Express composition seam created by CP-10.
- CP-12 depends on CP-09 through CP-11 but initially uses an injected readiness probe.

Checkpoint B:

- The app is importable without listening on a port.
- Invalid configuration fails before listen.
- Liveness, readiness, request IDs, 404s, validation errors, and unexpected errors satisfy the approved contract.

### Phase C — PostgreSQL infrastructure and high-risk reliability primitives

Goal: fail fast on the areas most likely to cause expensive rework: Supabase-compatible connectivity, repeatable migrations, audit persistence, and concurrent idempotency.

Tasks:

- CP-13 Prisma/PostgreSQL foundation and initial migration.
- CP-14 Durable audit-log slice.
- CP-15 Idempotency persistence and atomic-claim behavior.
- CP-16 Idempotency HTTP middleware and replay behavior.

Order:

- CP-13 is the prerequisite for CP-14 and CP-15.
- CP-16 depends on both CP-11 HTTP contracts and CP-15 persistence.
- CP-14 and CP-15 may run in parallel after the migration contract is stable.

Checkpoint C:

- Migrations apply to an empty PostgreSQL database.
- Audit writes are append-only through the application interface and redacted.
- Concurrent identical idempotency attempts execute one winner.
- Mismatched payload and in-flight duplicate behavior match the spec.

### Phase D — Contract generation, security, and observability

Goal: turn the backend foundation into a consumable, diagnosable, and hardened platform.

Tasks:

- CP-17 Deterministic OpenAPI 3.1 generation and contract tests.
- CP-18 Structured logging and request correlation.
- CP-19 RED metrics and optional OpenTelemetry bootstrap.
- CP-20 HTTP security, CORS, size limits, timeout, and rate-limit baseline.

Order and coordination:

- CP-17 depends on CP-11/12 so it can document real common responses.
- CP-18 precedes CP-19 because metrics/traces use the same normalized route and request context.
- CP-20 depends on CP-11 and must preserve the standard error envelope.
- CP-17 and CP-18 may proceed in parallel after Checkpoint B.

Checkpoint D:

- OpenAPI regeneration is byte-for-byte deterministic.
- Induced failures are discoverable by request ID without exposing secrets or PII.
- RED metrics use bounded labels.
- Security controls return the common error shape and pass focused tests.

### Phase E — External provider boundaries

Goal: prove the vendor boundaries while keeping the foundation fully testable offline.

Tasks:

- CP-21 Supabase Storage contract, fake, and adapter.
- CP-22 Resend email contract, fake, and adapter.
- CP-23 Gemini image contract, fake, and adapter.

Parallelization:

- All three tasks may proceed in parallel after CP-09, CP-18, and CP-20.
- No task performs a billable/live request in automated tests.

Checkpoint E:

- SDK types do not escape `src/integrations`.
- Every adapter validates provider output, applies timeouts, and maps failures to stable internal errors.
- Fake adapters cover success, invalid response, timeout, and refusal/transient-failure paths.

### Phase F — Typed clients in three repositories

Goal: demonstrate that all clients consume one immutable backend contract without importing backend source.

Tasks:

- CP-24 Public Web generated schema and API wrapper.
- CP-25 Management Web generated schema and API wrapper.
- CP-26 Expo generated schema and API wrapper.

Order and parallelization:

- All three depend on CP-17.
- They may run in parallel after the first stable committed OpenAPI artifact.
- The wrappers must normalize timeout, request ID, base URL, and API error handling consistently while remaining repo-local.

Checkpoint F:

- All three `api:generate` commands produce committed generated files with the same source digest.
- All three `api:check` commands fail on intentional drift and pass when regenerated.
- No client package imports `wedding-be/src`.

### Phase G — Automated quality gates and handoff documentation

Goal: make the platform reproducible on every pull request and understandable to the next module implementation.

Tasks:

- CP-27 Backend GitHub Actions quality and PostgreSQL integration pipeline.
- CP-28 Public Web GitHub Actions quality pipeline.
- CP-29 Management Web GitHub Actions quality pipeline.
- CP-30 Expo GitHub Actions quality pipeline.
- CP-31 Four-repository developer and environment documentation.
- CP-32 Final cross-repository acceptance audit.

Parallelization:

- CP-27 through CP-30 may proceed in parallel once their repository commands are stable.
- CP-31 can start after the relevant commands/configuration stop changing.
- CP-32 is strictly last.

Checkpoint G:

- Every pull request and push to `main` runs install, lint, typecheck, tests, build, and dependency audit.
- Backend CI additionally runs migrations and integration tests against PostgreSQL.
- The final audit maps evidence to all 12 success criteria in the approved spec.

## 6. Verification Model

Every implementation task must satisfy its focused checks before the next dependent task begins. Checkpoints then run the broader repository suites.

Required repository gates:

```bash
npm ci
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm run test
npm run test:coverage
npm run build
npm audit --audit-level=high
```

Additional backend gates:

```bash
npm run test:integration
npm run test:contract
npm run db:migrate:deploy
npm run api:check
```

Additional client gates:

```bash
npm run api:check
```

Additional Expo gate:

```bash
npx expo-doctor
```

The EAS preview cloud build remains a later `release-demo` acceptance action; this plan only establishes and validates its configuration.

## 7. Commit and Review Strategy

- Keep one short-lived branch per repository using `codex/core-platform`.
- Commit each verified task or tightly coupled pair as an atomic save point.
- Use `chore:` for toolchain/config, `feat:` for runtime platform primitives, `test:` for standalone test additions, and `docs:` for documentation.
- Do not combine generated scaffold formatting with behavioral code in one review commit when they can be separated.
- Commit generated artifacts required by the spec: npm lockfiles, Prisma migrations, `openapi/openapi.json`, and client schema declarations.
- Never commit `.env*` secrets, build outputs, test reports, Expo credentials, or service-account files.
- Cross-repository contract changes land backend-first, followed by coordinated client commits referencing the OpenAPI digest.

## 8. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Four repositories drift in Node, TypeScript, lint, or scripts | High | Pin the baseline, use equivalent script names, and enforce each repo through CI |
| OpenAPI artifact and runtime validation diverge | High | Generate from the same Zod schemas and fail `api:check` on any diff |
| Client CI cannot access a sibling backend repository | High | Supply an artifact from an immutable backend commit/release and verify its digest |
| Supabase connection mode is wrong for Prisma Migrate | High | Test direct/session URLs explicitly; prohibit transaction mode for migrations |
| Idempotency check/act race duplicates money or messages | High | Use a unique database constraint, atomic insert, and real concurrent PostgreSQL tests |
| Provider SDK details leak into domain code | Medium | Keep SDK imports inside adapters and test against local provider interfaces/fakes |
| Logs expose PII or tokens | High | Field allowlists, serializer redaction, and tests that inspect emitted logs |
| In-memory rate limiting silently weakens after scaling | High | Declare one-replica constraint; block horizontal scale until a shared store is designed |
| Expo dependency versions become incompatible | Medium | Install Expo-managed packages with `npx expo install` and gate on `expo-doctor` |
| CI becomes slow and is bypassed | Medium | Run static gates first, parallelize independent jobs, cache npm, target under 10 minutes |
| Exact Gemini model changes before invitation work | Low | Keep the model identifier in environment configuration behind `AiImageProvider` |
| Empty repos encourage oversized first commits | Medium | Follow the task slices and checkpoint after every 2–4 tasks |
| Restricted prospect access accidentally exposes full Couple features | High | Specify explicit entitlements, deny-by-default backend authorization, and direct endpoint tests before UI work |
| Timeline edit races with approval or payment initiation | High | Bind approvals to immutable revisions and add transactional concurrency tests at the booking/payment boundary |
| Private wedding media leaks through public invitation assets | High | Separate private object purposes, use short-lived signed access, and test cross-booking/public denial |
| Guest and seating ownership creates a dependency cycle | High | Keep guest-group identity in `guest-rsvp`; consume it from `seating-plan` without reverse imports |
| Concurrent arrivals lose or double-count attendance | High | Store append-only arrival/correction records and test real concurrent updates |
| Approved print content or price changes silently | High | Snapshot printable and commercial revisions atomically when the Couple approves the quotation |

## 9. Inputs Deferred Without Blocking This Plan

- Live Supabase credentials and final bucket identifiers.
- Resend verified sender domain.
- Gemini API key and selected production image model.
- EAS account/project ID and Android application identifier.
- Production hosting providers, domains, and telemetry exporter.
- Workspace invitation lifetime and reissue limits.
- Wedding-media MIME, size, dimension, quota, and cutoff policies.
- Timeline item limits and notification lead times.
- Layout capacity ranges and Manager exception-reason policy.
- Print quotation expiry, cancellation deadline, paper/finish catalog, and fulfillment service levels.
- Guest-search ranking and duplicate-name escalation procedure.

Fake adapters and placeholder `.env.example` values keep these inputs from blocking local implementation. Live integration smoke tests are scheduled only after the owner supplies credentials and authorizes external calls.

## 10. Core-Platform Approval Gate

The original approval authorizes work on `core-platform` only. CP-01 through CP-32 and their checkpoints remain unchanged in meaning; later capabilities still require their own approved specs, detailed vertical slices, and human approval.

## 11. Post-Core Contract and Dependency Graph

```text
CP-32 + core-platform implementation approval
        |
SPEC-01 identity-access spec and detailed plan
        |
identity-access implementation + evidence approval
        |
SPEC-02 venue-catalog spec and detailed plan
        |
venue-catalog implementation + evidence approval
        |
SPEC-03 booking-lifecycle final approval
        |
SPEC-04 payments-billing final approval
        |

implementation is complete. Final contract approval remains provider-first according
to the graph. After a module SPEC is approved, its plan and small vertical task slices

integration requires real providers. A completed draft never authorizes implementation
by itself.

## 13. Cross-Module Verification Checkpoints

### Access and commercial checkpoint

- A restricted prospect can collaborate on timeline revisions but receives backend denial from media, guest, seating, invitation, and print endpoints.
- The same identity gains full Couple access only after successful deposit.
- Payment initiation fails when the latest timeline revision lacks both active approvals.

### Planning and print checkpoint

- Private media is isolated by booking and never reachable from the generic public invitation.
- Guest-group identity remains stable across invitation households and fixed-layout table labels.
- Print approval freezes design, timeline, seating, QR, and commercial revisions before the charge enters receivables.

### Event-operations checkpoint

- Separate and concurrent arrivals accumulate correctly, over-expected attendance warns without blocking, and corrections remain auditable.
- Staff guide guests by group/color without per-person table or seat assignments.
- The generic physical-invitation QR cannot identify a guest, RSVP for a guest, or mutate check-in state.

## 14. Post-Core Planning Rules

- Each `SPEC-<module-id>.md` must cover objective, commands, project structure, code style, testing strategy, boundaries, state transitions, security/privacy, retention, and success criteria.
- Every owned requirement ID from `PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md` must map to at least one acceptance criterion and one planned automated test.
- Detailed implementation tasks must be vertical slices, normally touch no more than five human-authored files, identify dependencies, and include focused plus checkpoint verification.
- Provider interfaces and OpenAPI changes are fixed before consumer UI tasks may run in parallel.
- No task may silently reintroduce per-person seating, editable layout geometry, printed recipient names, per-recipient physical QR codes, or QR check-in.

readiness gate.

### 16.3 Verification checkpoints

**Checkpoint I1 — Authentication core:** IA-02 through IA-07 must pass unit,
PostgreSQL integration, concurrency, audit, redaction, lint, typecheck, and coverage
checks. No HTTP or client work proceeds with a failing credential/session primitive.

**Checkpoint I2 — Identity contracts:** IA-08 through IA-12 must prove every state
transition, denial, replay, and provider contract before the OpenAPI artifact is fixed.
The review specifically checks that `booking-lifecycle` and `payments-billing` depend on
identity-owned ports without a reverse import.

**Checkpoint I3 — Identity implementation approval:** IA-17 records all backend and
client evidence. The project owner must approve the completed module before SPEC-02 or
any `venue-catalog` implementation begins.

### 16.4 Risks and controls

| Risk | Control fixed by the draft |
| --- | --- |
| Stolen/replayed refresh credential | Opaque hashes, atomic rotation, absolute expiry, immediate family revocation on reuse. |
| Invitation used as permanent login | Single-use bootstrap, password verification/set, real revocable session, raw token removed from the URL fragment. |
| Duplicate identity during deposit promotion | Unique normalized account/access records and an idempotent monotonic provider port. |
| Full access without Couple role | Promotion atomically upserts `COUPLE`; restricted invitation acceptance never does. |
| Client-side role or access forgery | Actor and scoped access are rebuilt from current PostgreSQL state on every protected request. |
| Enumeration and credential stuffing | Generic outcomes, bounded per-IP/email throttling, no permanent attacker-triggered lockout. |
| PII or credential leakage | Allowlisted audit/metrics, core redaction tests, no browser durable storage, hash-only persistence. |
| Cross-repository contract drift | Backend-first OpenAPI generation plus immutable digest checks in all three clients. |
| Overlarge identity change | Small ordered slices and mandatory I1/I2/I3 review points. |

### 16.5 Parallelization and stop conditions

- IA-02 and IA-03 may run in parallel after IA-01 because neither consumes the other's
  implementation.
- IA-09 may begin after account and session revocation contracts are fixed; it does not
  need invitation code.
- IA-14, IA-15, and IA-16 may run in parallel only after IA-13 publishes the exact
  immutable OpenAPI artifact.
- Stop and return to H1 if a task needs a different auth provider, token transport,
  password policy, role model, cookie/CORS policy, retention period, external store, or
  new PII field.
- Stop and split a task if its reviewed human-authored file group exceeds the stated
  small-slice boundary or combines schema, HTTP, and multi-client behavior in one step.

### 17.4 Risks and controls

| Risk | Control fixed by the plan |
| --- | --- |
| Published price or template changes retroactively | Immutable exact versions, consumer snapshots, and historical-resolution tests. |
| Two Manager tabs publish conflicting versions | Draft CAS, transactional next-version assignment, idempotency, and PostgreSQL race tests. |
| Hall/layout capacity mismatch | Server recomputation, database ownership constraints, and capacity-lowering conflict tests. |
| Table labels point to a different physical table | Template-owned UUID registry, no ID recycling, exact layout version references. |
| Couple or forged UI mutates geometry | No Couple mutation operation in OpenAPI and direct backend role-denial tests. |
| Retiring catalog content breaks bookings or reports | New-selection exclusion separated from exact historical resolution; no hard deletion. |
| Catalog upload weakens private storage | Purpose-scoped generated keys, existing validation baseline, signed reads, failure cleanup. |
| Client drifts from backend rules | Backend-first immutable OpenAPI digest and generated Management Web types. |
| Layout editor is inaccessible or mobile-unusable | Keyboard controls, numeric field alternative, semantic forms, and responsive preview tests. |
| Oversized catalog change becomes unreviewable | Small vertical slices, five-file boundary, and V1/V2/V3/V4 review points. |

## 18. Fast-track planning protocol for SPEC-03 through SPEC-11

Beginning with `booking-lifecycle`, specifications are compact delta specs over the
already approved platform contracts and active `WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.1.0`. They must declare
that baseline version, list produced/consumed contracts and events, and must not repeat established environment,
HTTP/error, RBAC, audit, idempotency, pagination, migration, Storage, observability, or
secret-handling rules unless the module intentionally tightens one.

Drafting may overlap, but final approval follows `03 → 04 → 05 → 06`, then
`07 → 08 → 10` in parallel with `09`; `11` waits for both branches. Parallelism is
optional, not a target that overrides review capacity, file ownership, migration
ordering, or integration safety.

### 18.1 Wave budgets

| Module class | Modules | Planned waves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High-risk state/money/media | `booking-lifecycle`, `payments-billing`, `invitation-studio` | At most 8 |
| Product workflow | `guest-rsvp`, `seating-plan`, `staff-operations` | 4–6 |
| Operations/reporting/release | `notifications-automation`, `analytics-dashboard`, `release-demo` | 4–6 |

Every wave owns a coherent vertical outcome and keeps its detailed microtasks as
acceptance checklists. Microtasks do not become separate approval gates or trigger a
complete repository suite. A module normally uses these outcomes: decision/contract
lock, persistence/domain, services/authorization, HTTP/OpenAPI, independent clients,
and final acceptance; high-risk modules may split persistence, external providers, or
concurrency into additional waves within the budget.

### 18.2 Verification and continuation

- Focused tests and changed-file format/diff checks run inside each wave.
- Full repository gates run once at the module contract checkpoint.
- Clean migrations, deterministic seed, critical E2E, security/redaction, and evidence
  run once at final module acceptance.
- Independent aggregates or clients may proceed concurrently only after their provider
  or OpenAPI surface is stable and their worktrees/files do not overlap.
- Green waves continue without another owner round-trip. Stop only for a new business
  decision, dependency reversal, money/auth/history/schema safety exception, failed
  checkpoint, or final owner approval.

### 18.3 Rolling-plan rule

After a SPEC decision gate is approved, record its compact implementation waves in
`tasks/todo.md`; plans for separate approved SPECs may be prepared concurrently.
Reference the baseline and existing platform decisions instead of duplicating them,

| Media list/detail/original download | GET `/bookings/{id}/media`, GET `/bookings/{id}/media/{assetId}`, POST `/management/bookings/{id}/media/{assetId}/download-links` | Own FULL/authorized Manager; download link only for authorized original use; no arbitrary key/public original. |
| Media policy read/change | GET `/bookings/{id}/media-policy`, PATCH `/management/bookings/{id}/media-policy` | Couple read; Manager audited cutoff/policyRevision command, expected revision/intent; not a mutation bypass. |

| AI request | POST `/bookings/{id}/invitation-image-generations` | Own FULL; bounded approved prompt/one output; durable intent, UNKNOWN/reconciliation, no automatic paid retry. |
| Unpublish | DELETE `/bookings/{id}/invitations/{designId}/publication` | Own FULL/authorized Manager, revision/intent; concealed public404 and preserved history; event representation reviewed. |
| Print list/detail | GET `/bookings/{id}/print-orders[/{orderId}]`; Manager GET `/management/print-orders[/{orderId}]` | Bounded private list, quote/accepted history/status; no client-authoritative totals. |

| Cancel request/quote / approved order | POST `/bookings/{id}/print-orders/{orderId}/cancellation`; POST `/management/print-orders/{orderId}/cancellation` | Before approval own Couple/Manager, no charge; approved only Manager/pre-production with Couple confirmation and accepted billing credit. |
| Replacement proposal/approval | POST `/management/print-orders/{orderId}/replacement-proposals`; POST `/bookings/{id}/print-orders/{orderId}/replacement-approvals` | Manager proposal+renewed Couple approval before production; new full charge/old credit atomic or pending with production blocked; preserve old effective revision. |

### CP-15: Implement atomic idempotency persistence

**Description:** Build canonical request hashing, atomic database claims, state transitions, retention timestamps, and concurrency tests independent of Express.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [x] `(namespace, idempotencyKey)` uniqueness atomically selects one winner.
- [x] Canonical hashing is deterministic and detects same-key/different-payload use.
- [x] Real concurrent PostgreSQL tests show exactly one successful claim.

**Verification:**

- [x] `npm run test:unit -- idempotency-hash`
- [x] `npm run test:integration -- idempotency-repository`
- [x] Repeat the concurrency test enough times to detect a check-then-insert race.

**Implementation evidence (2026-09-29):** Canonical request hashing now recursively sorts object keys, preserves array order and JSON scalar types, produces lowercase SHA-256 digests, and rejects cyclic, sparse, non-finite, symbol-bearing, or otherwise non-JSON payloads. The typed idempotency service validates printable 1–128 byte keys, calculates injectable 30-day default and explicit 180-day payment retention timestamps, distinguishes `CLAIMED`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `MISMATCH`, `SUCCEEDED`, and `FAILED`, and permits only one terminal transition. The Prisma repository attempts `create` without a preceding read, lets the existing compound unique constraint choose the winner, resolves `P2002` to that winning row, and guards terminal updates with `id + IN_PROGRESS`; focused unit tests cover Prisma error propagation and terminal-state immutability. The idempotency-only unit suite passes 45 tests and scoped coverage is 100% statements, branches, functions, and lines; the exact hash verification command passes 10 tests. The initial Prisma migration was deployed to Supabase and its migration status is current. Against that real PostgreSQL database, the integration suite passes all 22 tests, including 20 rounds of 12 simultaneous claims that each produce exactly one winner and one stored row, plus a concurrent terminal-transition race that preserves retention timestamps. The stress rounds run in batches of four and retain all 240 claim attempts; the complete 165-test suite passes through the Supabase session pooler in about 69 seconds. Timed-out diagnostic rows were removed and no test namespaces remain. Strict typecheck, ESLint, Prettier, and the production build pass. `npm audit` still reports the pre-existing Prisma CLI/configuration findings in `deepmerge-ts` and unused MySQL support (one moderate and four high findings); this slice adds no dependency or lockfile change, so the existing 2026-10-12/CP-32 review gate remains applicable.

**Estimated scope:** Medium

### CP-16: Add idempotency HTTP claim and replay behavior

**Description:** Connect the persistence primitive to explicitly marked routes while preserving validation-before-claim and unknown-outcome safety.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [x] Missing/invalid keys, in-flight duplicates, payload mismatch, and completed replay use documented status/error semantics.
- [x] Two concurrent HTTP requests execute the protected handler once.
- [x] Unknown external outcomes remain reconcilable and are never silently re-executed.

**Verification:**

- [x] `npm run test:integration -- idempotency-http`
- [x] `npm run test:coverage -- idempotency`
- [x] Inspect database state after forced success, deterministic failure, and simulated timeout.

**Implementation evidence (2026-09-30):** Explicit route-level middleware now reads and validates exactly one `Idempotency-Key`, derives a collision-safe namespace from trusted actor scope, HTTP method, normalized route, and operation version, and claims only after the route's request validator has succeeded. The documented contract returns `400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`, `422 INVALID_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY`, `422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`, or `409 REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS` with `Retry-After` as appropriate. Successful `2xx` and deterministic `4xx` JSON/no-content responses are persisted before transmission and replayed without re-running the handler; replayed standard error envelopes receive the current request ID, while successful domain payloads are left unchanged. `3xx` and `5xx` responses remain `IN_PROGRESS`, so a simulated provider timeout returns `504` once and a retry returns `409` without repeating the external effect. ## Fast-track protocol — SPEC-03 through SPEC-11

**Approval evidence (2026-10-05):** The project owner approved compact module planning
and continuous-wave implementation for every module beginning with SPEC-03. Module
dependency order and final owner approval remain unchanged.

**Contract lock evidence (2026-10-06):** The project owner approved and locked
`WEDDING-CONTRACT-1@1.0.0`. It applies to SPEC-03 through SPEC-11, leaves SPEC-02
unchanged through V4, and replaces the former fully sequential later-SPEC drafting
rule with the controlled gates below.

- Each module uses a delta specification: reference the approved core-platform,
  identity, audit, idempotency, error, pagination, migration, Storage, and security
  contracts instead of restating them.
- `booking-lifecycle`, `payments-billing`, and `invitation-studio` may use at most eight
  implementation waves because their state, money, and media risks are high. Later
  modules use four to six waves unless a documented dependency requires one more.
- Microtasks remain explicit as acceptance checklists inside their owning wave, but do
  not require separate owner approval or a separate full-suite run.
- Each wave runs focused proof while it is active. The complete repository gates run
  once at the module contract/checkpoint, and clean migration/seed/E2E/security evidence
  runs once at final module acceptance.
- Independent backend aggregates and client surfaces may proceed in parallel only after
  their provider/OpenAPI contract is stable and their files/worktrees do not overlap.
- Continue automatically between green waves. Stop for a new business decision,
  dependency-direction change, schema/history/money/auth safety exception, failed module
  gate, or final owner approval.

## Rolling-Plan Rule

When a SPEC task is approved, insert that module's compact implementation waves
after its specification gate; plans for separate approved SPECs may be prepared
concurrently. Record microtasks as acceptance checklists inside their owning wave
rather than expanding them into separately approved execution tasks. Link each
consumer integration wave to the real provider evidence it requires. Checklist order
does not override the dependency graph, serialized Prisma migration lane, or provider
acceptance gates. Never mark a SPEC task complete merely because a draft exists;
decision approval and wave insertion are required.

# Core-platform acceptance evidence

Audit date: 2026-10-03 (Asia/Saigon)

Scope: `wedding-be`, `wedding-web`, `wedding-manage-web`, and `wedding-app`

Status: **Accepted by the project owner on 2026-10-03**

The local acceptance audit is complete. The configured migration target is the
shared Supabase `postgres` database at `db.zjibuegbbwzvdqrnujjf.supabase.co`, so
the audit did not risk applying migrations to that root schema. Instead, it
created a disposable local PostgreSQL 17 database, ran the exact
`npm run db:migrate:deploy` command successfully, and removed the container
afterward. The isolated migration-policy integration test also ran against a
new schema on the configured PostgreSQL service, deployed all committed
migrations, proved a forward compensating migration, and removed the schema.

The project owner reviewed this evidence and explicitly approved
`core-platform` implementation on 2026-10-03. That approval opens the Phase H

# Identity-access acceptance evidence

Audit date: 2026-10-04 (Asia/Saigon)

Scope: `wedding-be`, `wedding-web`, `wedding-manage-web`, and `wedding-app`

Status: **Passed and approved at Checkpoint I3**

IA-17 was completed without opening SPEC-02. ACC-002 through ACC-007 have current
automated evidence, D1-D7 match runtime behavior, all repository gates pass, and the
previous D6, PostgreSQL, and Windows SWC blockers are resolved. On 2026-10-05 the
project owner explicitly instructed, “hãy hoàn tất Checkpoint I3,” approving the
completed implementation and this evidence. SPEC-02 specification/planning may now
begin; venue-catalog implementation still requires its own approved specification and
implementation plan.

## Audit environment and resolved blockers

- Node.js 24.15.0 and npm 11.7.0 satisfy the declared engine ranges.
- A disposable PostgreSQL 17 Docker container was exposed only on
  `127.0.0.1:55432`. Both committed migrations deployed from empty, all database and
  concurrency tests ran there, and the shared Supabase `public` schema was not used.
- The reusable Docker procedure and environment-variable boundary are recorded in
  `docs/cross-repo-development.md` for later acceptance runs.
- Four exact Node PIDs whose command lines belonged to the Public Web and Management
  Web `next dev` processes were stopped. This released
  `next-swc.win32-x64-msvc.node`; clean `npm ci` then passed in both repositories.
  The runbook records how to identify the owning process and prohibits blanket Node
  termination.
- Default multi-process Vitest workers were unstable on this Windows host: one backend
  process exited with `0xC0000409`, and simultaneous frontend fork pools timed out
  before loading tests. Serialized `threads` runs with one worker executed every test
  and passed. No failed assertion was hidden by the workaround.

## Repository gate results

Public and Management Web tests keep backend denial authoritative. |

## D1-D7 and checkpoint review

- D1, D3, D4, D5, and D7 match the passing unit, contract, PostgreSQL integration,
  configuration, and client behavior in this audit.
- D2 matches all clients: Web access state is memory-only, Web refresh is cookie-based,

  used for refresh credentials.
- D6 now has an operator-only executor in
  `src/modules/identity-access/account/identity-retention.ts` and
  `scripts/identity-retention.ts`. It locks the approved 180/30/90/365-day policy,
  selects only due disabled accounts, transactionally requires a fact for every linked
  consultation, honors active holds, anonymizes email/display PII, deletes password
  verifiers, revokes live auth material, sets `piiAnonymizedAt`, retains only the UUID
  as a pseudonymous business/audit reference, and deletes terminal identity metadata
  after its approved window.
- D6 workers use PostgreSQL `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`; the PostgreSQL race test proves
  one account produces one anonymization and one audit row. Account and terminal
  metadata cleanup are both bounded by `batchSize`; re-runs are idempotent.
- I1 and I2 concurrency claims were freshly revalidated in the full PostgreSQL run.
  The project owner approved I3 on 2026-10-05.

## Verdict

The three previously recorded blockers are closed:

1. D6 has a tested, idempotent PostgreSQL anonymization/cleanup executor.
2. A disposable PostgreSQL 17 Docker workflow now proves clean migrations and all
   concurrency/integration suites and is documented for reuse.
3. The exact Next.js processes holding the SWC binaries were stopped and both clean

IA-17 passes and the project owner has approved Checkpoint I3. SPEC-02
specification/planning may begin. This approval does not authorize venue-catalog

# Venue-catalog acceptance evidence

Audit date: 2026-10-06 (Asia/Saigon)

Scope: `wedding-be` FT-V1 through FT-V3 and `wedding-manage-web` FT-V4, VC-01
through VC-23

Status: **Passed at Checkpoint V4**

## Delivered contract and implementation

- The backend owns restaurant, shift, hall, dish/menu, timeline, fixed-layout, stable
  table identity, lifecycle, and private catalog-media authority. Public/current reads
  expose no draft, audit actor, object-key, or service-role fields.
- Manager mutations remain authenticated and authorized by the bearer session. The
  Management Web role presentation cannot manufacture authority and does not expose a
  Staff mutation path.
- Draft updates use server revisions. Published/superseded versions are immutable;
  cloning creates a separate draft. Integer VND values and layout totals are never
  calculated from floating-point client state.
- Layouts are hall-bound on a fixed `10000 x 10000` canvas. Numeric keyboard controls
  are the authoritative editor; there is no Couple geometry or per-guest seating
  operation.
- Catalog media is allowlisted to JPEG, PNG, and WebP with a 10 MB advisory client
  bound and authoritative backend validation. The UI stores only returned signed
  metadata, refreshes expiring URLs, and never renders an object key.

## SEA and decision trace

- **SEA-001:**
  `src/modules/venue-catalog/application/layout.service.test.ts` — “recomputes hall
  and seat bounds in the publication transaction”; and
  `tests/integration/venue-catalog/layout-behavior.test.ts` — “rejects a hall range
  above either current hall capacity or summed table seats”. The Management Web
  companion proof is
  `src/features/venue-catalog/layout-panel.test.tsx` — range/canvas validation blocks
  the API call and the editor displays hall maximum and current seat totals.
- **SEA-002:**
  `tests/integration/venue-catalog/layout-behavior.test.ts` — “publishes one winner,
  preserves exact history, and never reuses retired table IDs”; and
  `src/modules/venue-catalog/application/layout.service.test.ts` — stable IDs survive
  clone/history and retirement is irreversible. The Management Web companion proof
  preserves UUIDs during geometry edits and calls permanent retirement on removal.
- VC-D1 through VC-D9 still match the approved runtime behavior. Checkpoints V1 and
  V2 proved persistence/concurrency and service/provider boundaries; V3 proved the
  immutable HTTP/OpenAPI boundary. FT-V4 consumes only generated operations from that
  boundary.

## Contract lock

- Backend contract commit:
  `7b01f0b13c828a0caac719ae4a739c8d4e2a73b0`
- Generated artifact: `openapi/openapi.json`
- Current SHA-256:
  `caad010d6008cbfc8fc0748f49abad0c651e85ccda5cf008b60ac3f4e6fa3dc5`
- Management Web lock: `api-contract.lock.json`, generated client and schemas all
  report the same digest. The UI contract mark reads the lockfile digest rather than
  duplicating it as a hand-maintained string.
- V3 was initially frozen at digest
  `8aa21388cacb5d2ffa1cfd2cfb6ef5fa23b4964058a72143453bdc2b47215db8`.
  With explicit project-owner authorization, it was reopened only for the missing
  Manager restaurant/shift/hall reads and signed-media list read. Commits
  `6c48188c74d0b20d27f090629e15f01fda10d453` and
  `7b01f0b13c828a0caac719ae4a739c8d4e2a73b0` contain those additive operations.

The full coverage command used one worker and a 15-second per-test timeout because the

---
name: wedding-design-system
description: Design and implement UI for wedding-web, wedding-manage-web, and wedding-app with the approved garden-estate editorial visual system. Use for new or revised screens and shared components in these three products; do not use for backend-only work or unrelated brands.

# Wedding Design System

Apply the approved design direction autonomously across the Wedding Management ecosystem. Preserve each product's purpose while making the three surfaces feel like one brand.

## Required context

- Read [references/foundation.md](references/foundation.md) for every visual design or UI implementation task.
- Read [references/product-patterns.md](references/product-patterns.md) only for the product being changed.
- Read [references/taste-audit.md](references/taste-audit.md) when designing, implementing, or reviewing a visual change.
- Read [references/delivery-workflow.md](references/delivery-workflow.md) when implementing or reviewing code, not when only answering a conceptual question.

The prior screenshots in `assets/approved-samples/` are implementation and information-architecture anchors, not visual templates for the current system. Never transcribe their copy, typography, colors, imagery, or layout wholesale. Resolve visual decisions from the current references; resolve copy from the current product requirements, domain terminology, and Vietnamese-language quality instead.

## Product contract

- Use Vietnamese for user-facing copy unless the user requests another language.
- Keep the visual character garden-estate inspired: pressed-ivory canvas, laurel/forest structure, antique-champagne detail, soft-charcoal text, Be Vietnam Pro Vietnamese typography, Lora Latin wordmarks only, framed warm imagery, and generous whitespace.
- Do not copy third-party logos, wording, photography, or unique branded assets. Inspiration may inform composition and visual tone only.
- Prefer existing project components and tokens. Extend the central theme when a reusable decision is missing; do not scatter near-duplicate colors or spacing values through screens.
- Let the public website feel emotional and image-led, the management website operational and information-dense, and the mobile app intimate and native. Shared tokens create family resemblance; identical layouts do not.
- Maintain semantic HTML or native accessibility, visible focus, readable contrast, touch targets, responsive layouts, loading/empty/error states, and dark-mode behavior where the product already supports it.
- Use low-radius or square surfaces, hairline rules, tonal layers, and image mattes instead of heavy shadows. Reserve pills and fully rounded shapes for statuses, avatars, compact counters, and progress indicators.
- Prefer calm, useful motion only when it clarifies state. Respect reduced-motion preferences.
- Calibrate variance, motion, and density from the product baseline before composing a screen. These are decision aids, not quality scores or reasons to add novelty.

## Decision authority

The user has approved this system for subsequent Wedding screens. Make routine visual and composition decisions without requesting a new mockup approval. Ask only when requirements introduce a materially different brand direction, a missing product decision that changes behavior, or an irreversible external action.

When several layouts are valid, choose the one that best preserves content hierarchy, task clarity, and the product-specific pattern in the references. Do not invent novelty merely to make screens look different.

## Completion standard

A UI task is complete only when the relevant automated checks pass, the rendered result has been inspected at its target viewport, browser/runtime errors are absent, the taste pre-flight passes, and the screen remains consistent with the approved visual foundation and product pattern. Temporary photography is acceptable for prototypes but must be identified as replaceable before production.

# Visual foundation

## Brand character

The system should feel like a cultivated garden estate hosting an intimate celebration: quiet, tactile, romantic, and exceptionally composed. It combines editorial restraint with botanical warmth—pressed-ivory paper, laurel green structure, antique-champagne detail, and architectural image framing.

Avoid clinical white, digital-blue product chrome, generic SaaS gradients, glassmorphism, oversized rounded cards, heavy shadows, loud decorative motifs, and script fonts. Luxury comes from material contrast, whitespace, typography, and intentional imagery rather than ornament.

## Color tokens

Use these semantic roles rather than choosing colors screen by screen.

| Role | Light value | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Estate forest | `#334537` | Primary action, active navigation, dark structural bands |
| Deep evergreen | `#243B2A` | Hover/pressed state and the darkest structural surface |
| Laurel sage | `#4A5D4E` | Brand anchor, selected states, botanical emphasis |
| Antique champagne | `#C5A880` | Fine rules, image mattes, premium emphasis, small highlights |
| Earth | `#8C6D62` | Secondary celebratory accent; use sparingly |
| Pressed ivory | `#FAF8F5` | Page canvas and warm base surface |
| Alabaster | `#FFFFFF` | Raised card and form surface |
| Champagne dust | `#F3EFEA` | Muted sections, table headers, quiet panels |
| Soft charcoal | `#232321` | Primary body text |
| Muted charcoal | `#62645F` | Secondary text and inactive UI |
| Sage rule | `rgba(74, 93, 78, 0.12)` | Standard dividers and card outlines |
| Brass rule | `rgba(197, 168, 128, 0.35)` | Elevated frames and special dividers |

Use `#FAF8F5` or the closest existing semantic canvas token before adding a new background. Gold/champagne is a fine detail, never a large text background. Text and interactive states must meet WCAG AA contrast; do not use low-contrast champagne for small text.

Dark themes should preserve the same material relationship instead of mechanically inverting the palette. Recommended anchors: dark canvas `#1C211D`, raised surface `#28312A`, primary text `#F7F3EC`, muted text `#C9CDC6`, primary action `#B7CCB9`, and champagne detail `#E0C298`.

## Typography

- Vietnamese display, headings, body, and UI: `"Be Vietnam Pro", "Segoe UI", Arial, sans-serif`. Use its 400–600 weights and scale/whitespace—not artificial tracking—for hierarchy. This is the safe default for all Vietnamese copy, labels, forms, tables, and operational data.
- Latin-only wordmarks or a short Latin venue name may use `Lora, Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif` for an editorial note. Never apply Lora to Vietnamese content in browser UI: real Chromium rendering must take priority over a serif treatment.
- Labels and overlines: Be Vietnam Pro semibold. A small amount of tracking is optional for short ASCII labels; retain authored case and normal tracking for Vietnamese labels or any text containing diacritics.
- Use a script face only when the product already has an approved, Vietnamese-safe asset and the accent is optional. It is not part of the default system.
- Use Unicode NFC source text. Do not transform Vietnamese copy to uppercase in CSS and do not apply `letter-spacing` to Vietnamese text: both can disrupt diacritic shaping or produce visibly separated words. Keep `font-kerning: normal` and common ligatures enabled.
- Verify representative Vietnamese diacritics in a rendered browser/device, including `quyết định`, `tiếp tục`, `kế hoạch`, and `đầy đủ`. Do not allow a serif heading to clip, split Vietnamese words, or force a fallback face unexpectedly.

Suggested hierarchy: display 56/68 desktop and 38/46 mobile; display-small 40/50 desktop and 28/36 mobile; headline 32/40, 24/32, 20/28; body 18/28, 15/24, 13/20; labels 13/18, 11/16, 10/14. Treat these as roles, not a reason to force every size into every screen.

## Shape, border, and depth

- Web surfaces use a 2–4px radius. Mobile may use 4–12px where native ergonomics benefit, without turning every section into a card.
- Favor 1px sage rules for standard grouping and antique-champagne rules for image mats, premium summaries, and significant dividers.
- A framed image may use an outer champagne rule and 8–16px ivory matte. An arched top is allowed only for a primary feature image when it strengthens the venue story.
- Shadows are rare and diffuse: cards may use `0 4px 20px -2px rgba(35, 35, 33, 0.04)`; overlays may use `0 16px 40px -8px rgba(35, 35, 33, 0.08)`. Prefer tonal layers, rules, and whitespace first.
- Fully rounded shapes are limited to statuses, avatars, counters, and progress indicators. Default tags are compact rectangles with minimal rounding.

## Spacing and density

Use a 4/8-point rhythm. Typical editorial spacing: 6px, 12px, 20px, 36px, and 56px; desktop page margins 64px with 32px gutters; mobile page margins 24px with 16px gutters. Use a fluid 12-column desktop grid (max 1380px), 8-column tablet grid, and 4-column mobile grid.

Marketing and invitation views should have generous vertical pauses and occasional narrow reading columns. Operational views should be compact through alignment and systematic grouping, not smaller text. Align major edges across page headers, imagery, summaries, tables, and actions.

## Imagery

- Choose warm, editorial images of Vietnamese weddings, refined venues, flowers, celebrations, or food when relevant to the content.
- Favor one large, well-matted focal photograph over a collage of decorative images. Crop intentionally and test desktop and mobile aspect ratios.
- Use a low-opacity ivory or forest overlay only when needed for readable text; preserve the image's atmosphere.
- Prototype photography must be replaceable. Production uses project-owned or explicitly licensed assets with meaningful alt text when the image conveys content.

## Interaction and accessibility

- Primary buttons are estate forest with pressed-ivory text, rectangular/low-radius, uppercase semibold labels, and enough padding for a 44px target. Hover deepens toward evergreen; never rely on letter-spacing animation as the only feedback.
- Secondary actions use a sage or champagne hairline with charcoal text; editorial links use a subtle underlined text treatment and may include a trailing arrow.
- Every form control has a visible label, useful help/error text, a clear forest focus state, and a stable disabled state. Inputs are lightly framed or bottom-ruled—not floating rounded capsules.
- Preserve heading order, landmarks, accessible names, keyboard navigation, live regions for async status, and a deliberate narrow-screen strategy for data tables.
- Respect reduced-motion preferences. Motion should clarify state, not delay access to booking, RSVP, operational data, or forms.
```
