```text
# Product patterns

Read only the section for the product being changed. The prior screenshots in `../assets/approved-samples/` may be used to understand established information architecture and product behavior; they are not visual templates for this updated system.

## `wedding-web`

Purpose: emotional public and couple-facing experiences such as invitations, discovery, wedding details, and guest interactions.

Taste baseline: **variance 6, motion 3–4, density 3**. Routine forms may lower variance and motion; major editorial or campaign pages may raise variance by one. Preserve clarity and keep the primary action obvious.

Preferred composition:

- A slim muted or champagne-dust announcement strip only when it carries meaningful context.
- A calm editorial header: Latin wordmark may use Lora; Vietnamese navigation and actions use Be Vietnam Pro.
- A full-bleed or split hero with warm photography, restrained ivory/forest overlay only where copy needs it, and a concise Be Vietnam Pro statement.
- Pressed-ivory canvas, asymmetrical but balanced editorial sections, measured photo mattes, and hairline rules instead of decorative color bands.
- Short labels used selectively; serif section titles; Be Vietnam Pro body copy at a comfortable reading width. Do not force Vietnamese labels or headings to uppercase.
- Alabaster fact or RSVP groups with sage borders; champagne is reserved for framing and small emphasis.
- One dominant action per section. Vary page rhythm to match the story rather than repeating a card grid.

On mobile, stack image before content, keep primary facts visible, reduce display type, and turn multi-column fact/form groups into one column. Do not reproduce desktop navigation at reduced scale.

Approved anchor: `../assets/approved-samples/wedding-web.png`.

## `wedding-manage-web`

Purpose: fast operational work for managers and staff. Beauty supports scanability; it must not obscure state or actions.

Taste baseline: **variance 3, motion 2, density 7**. Operational consistency takes priority over novelty. Increase density through hierarchy, grids, and progressive disclosure rather than smaller text.

Preferred composition:

- Deep evergreen or estate-forest sidebar/navigation with a restrained champagne active rule; avoid bright-blue application chrome.
- Be Vietnam Pro page titles paired with compact operational metadata and controls; reserve Lora for a Latin-only wordmark.
- Pressed-ivory canvas with alabaster work surfaces, champagne-dust table/panel headers, sage row separators, and clear alignment.
- Square or barely rounded metric cells with thin sage/champagne rules instead of floating card stacks.
- A featured venue/event strip may combine forest copy with one framed image, only when it surfaces relevant work.
- Compact rectangular status tags that pair color with text/icon; no decorative pills or vague synthetic metrics.
- Dense but readable tables on desktop; deliberate column prioritization on narrow screens.
- Timelines and attention queues use alignment, time, and small color markers instead of large decorative cards.

Keep controls predictable and close to the data they affect. Use confirmation for consequential actions and expose system status without visual noise.

Approved anchor: `../assets/approved-samples/wedding-manage-web.png`.

## `wedding-app`

Purpose: an intimate planning companion for a couple, optimized for quick progress checks and the next useful action.

Taste baseline: **variance 4, motion 3, density 5**. Branded moments may be expressive, but navigation, forms, sheets, and touch behavior remain native and predictable.

Preferred composition:

- A compact Latin Lora wordmark or a Be Vietnam Pro screen title, followed by a warm hero or a content-led first action—not a mandatory marketing layout.
- Pressed-ivory canvas, estate-forest date/venue or progress anchors, and champagne hairlines for important grouping.
- A centered welcome/milestone block with a short Be Vietnam Pro title, calm body copy, and a thin divider; no default script accent.
- Champagne-dust planning or appointment panels with thin sage/champagne borders.
- Task lists built from separators, order, and clear completion affordances rather than a stack of rounded cards.
- Appointment or milestone sections in powder blue.
- Native controls and platform behavior; use the existing Expo theme, `expo-image`, and native-capable UI components already present in the project.

Support dynamic color/dark mode through semantic tokens. Important dates and values may be selectable. Keep scroll behavior, safe areas, touch targets, and Android rendering in the verification loop.

Approved anchor: `../assets/approved-samples/wedding-app.png`.

## Cross-product reuse

Reuse semantic tokens, typography roles, status meanings, field patterns, and content terminology. Share implementation packages only when the repositories already support that architecture; do not force cross-repository coupling merely to avoid a few duplicated constants.
```

```text
# Wedding taste audit

This is a curated anti-generic design layer for the Wedding products. It is not a dependency on another skill and must not override the approved brand foundation, product behavior, accessibility, or the existing technology stack.

## Three decision dials

The dials describe how a screen should behave visually. They are not quality scores.

| Dial | Low values | High values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Variance | Familiar, symmetric, predictable composition | More editorial, asymmetric, and varied composition |
| Motion | Static UI with essential feedback | Choreographed transitions and scroll-linked effects |
| Density | Few elements and generous whitespace | More information and actions per viewport |

Start from the product baseline:

| Product | Variance | Motion | Density |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `wedding-web` | 6 | 3–4 | 3 |
| `wedding-manage-web` | 3 | 2 | 7 |
| `wedding-app` | 4 | 3 | 5 |

Adjust at most one or two points when the screen type clearly warrants it. Examples:

- A campaign or venue story page may use `7 / 4 / 2`.
- A public account form may use `4 / 2 / 4`.
- A management command center may use `3 / 2 / 8`.
- A management configuration form may use `2 / 1 / 6`.
- Mobile onboarding may use `5 / 4 / 3`.
- A mobile task list may use `3 / 2 / 6`.

If a design needs to move farther than two points from its product baseline, reconsider whether the composition belongs to that product before proceeding.

## Pre-design read

Before composing a screen, identify internally:

1. the product and primary audience;
2. the single most important user task;
3. whether this is greenfield, a preservation redesign, or a functional overhaul;
4. the real content, states, assets, and constraints already present;
5. the chosen dial values and why they differ from the baseline, if they do.

Do not emit a ceremonial design-plan block or ask the user to tune the dials. State an assumption only when it materially affects the result.

For redesigns, inspect before changing. Preserve working routes, navigation labels, form names, legal copy, domain terminology, and behavior unless the task explicitly authorizes a change.

## Anti-default sweep

Use these as diagnostic questions, not universal bans:

- Are three equal cards being used simply because they are easy?
- Do consecutive sections repeat the same left-text/right-image or centered-heading pattern?
- Has every content group been placed inside a rounded card?
- Does nearly every heading have a tiny uppercase eyebrow above it?
- Are decorative pills, status dots, fake metrics, or badges present without helping the task?
- Does the copy use vague claims, generic names, filler language, or implausibly perfect numbers?
- Are gradients, glass effects, shadows, and animation being used to manufacture “premium” rather than support hierarchy?
- Is a stock image visually unrelated to the Vietnamese wedding context or the content beside it?
- Is the interface merely imitating the approved sample instead of solving the new information hierarchy?

When the answer is yes, remove the pattern or replace it with a task-specific composition. Do not introduce novelty solely to avoid repetition.

## Consistency locks

Audit each rendered screen for these locks:

- **Color:** every color has a semantic role from the Wedding palette. Gold remains detail, navy remains structure/action, and powder blue remains a quiet surface.
- **Shape:** square and low-radius surfaces dominate; pills remain limited to compact statuses, counters, avatars, and progress.
- **Typography:** display serif, restrained script, and body sans retain their assigned roles. Vietnamese glyphs render cleanly.
- **Iconography:** one coherent icon family or the platform-native set is used within a product surface. Icons are not hand-drawn merely for differentiation.
- **Motion:** durations and easing form a small consistent vocabulary. Reduced-motion behavior is present when motion exceeds basic state feedback.
- **Terminology:** the same domain concept uses the same Vietnamese label across web, management, and mobile where roles align.

## Product-specific taste checks

### `wedding-web`

- The opening viewport has one clear message and one dominant action.
- Display headings normally remain within two or three lines and Vietnamese words do not clip or break unnaturally.
- CTA labels remain on one line at desktop widths.
- Photography is intentional, well-cropped, and strong enough to justify its space.
- Consecutive sections vary their rhythm without becoming stylistically unrelated.
- Motion supports storytelling but never delays access to forms, pricing, RSVP, or event details.
- Decorative labels and script accents are used sparingly.

### `wedding-manage-web`

- Navigation, filters, bulk actions, tables, and pagination appear where an operator expects them.
- Density comes from alignment and hierarchy, not reduced readability or cramped touch targets.
- Tables have a narrow-screen strategy and do not silently hide critical actions.
- Status never relies on color alone and uses a stable vocabulary.
- Loading, empty, error, permission-denied, destructive, and success states are designed when reachable.
- Motion is limited to feedback and spatial continuity; data should not animate for spectacle.
- Brand styling does not obscure scanning, sorting, filtering, or comparison.

### `wedding-app`

- Navigation, forms, sheets, back behavior, safe areas, and touch feedback feel native.
- Primary touch targets are approximately 44px or larger.
- The first viewport answers “what matters next?” without reproducing the entire plan.
- Branded moments such as countdowns and milestones do not turn routine workflows into marketing pages.
- Motion uses platform-friendly transforms/opacity and remains smooth on mid-range Android devices.
- Dynamic color or dark-mode tokens preserve hierarchy and contrast.
- Long screens have deliberate grouping and scrolling; content is not fragmented into excessive cards.

## Final taste pre-flight

Before delivery, verify the rendered result:

- [ ] Dial values fit the product and screen type.
- [ ] The primary action and hierarchy are obvious without explanation.
- [ ] No repeated generic layout or card pattern dominates the screen.
- [ ] Color, shape, typography, icon, motion, and terminology locks pass.
- [ ] CTA text, form labels, helper text, errors, and focus states meet contrast requirements.
- [ ] Vietnamese text does not clip, overflow, orphan badly, or break inside words.
- [ ] Loading, empty, error, disabled, success, and destructive states exist where relevant.
- [ ] The target viewport and one adjacent breakpoint have been inspected.
- [ ] Browser/runtime logs contain no unresolved errors.
- [ ] No new UI framework, animation library, icon package, or font dependency was assumed without checking the repository and justifying the addition.

## Deliberate exclusions

Do not import these general-purpose taste patterns into the Wedding system:

- forced random layout selection;
- mandatory AIDA page structure;
- mandatory Tailwind, shadcn, GSAP, Motion, or a specific icon package;
- mandatory image generation before direct implementation;
- blanket bans on serif typography or warm cream/gold/brown palettes;
- animation or texture added to every section;
- rules that exclude dashboards, data tables, forms, or native mobile.

The approved serif and estate palette are explicit brand decisions, not generic defaults. The management dashboard and native mobile app are first-class Wedding products and require their own product patterns.

## Influence and license

The audit approach and dial vocabulary were adapted and substantially rewritten for this project after reviewing [Taste Skill](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill) and its audit-oriented variants. Taste Skill is published under the [MIT License](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill/blob/main/LICENSE), Copyright (c) 2026 Leonxlnx. The external repository is not installed, invoked, or updated automatically by this skill.
```

````text
# Delivery workflow

## 1. Establish the screen contract

Inspect the target repository, existing routes/components/theme, nearby tests, and any task acceptance criteria. Identify the primary user, primary action, essential states, and target breakpoints before composing the screen.

Use the approved system without requesting routine visual approval. The current visual authority is `foundation.md` plus the relevant product pattern; legacy screenshots are behavior/information-architecture anchors only. When the task leaves minor copy or layout choices open, make a coherent product decision and document only material assumptions.

## 2. Calibrate and audit the direction

Read the relevant product baseline in `product-patterns.md`, adjust the three taste dials only when the screen type warrants it, and run the pre-design checks in `taste-audit.md`. Treat the chosen values as constraints on composition, not as requirements to add visual effects.

For redesigns, audit the current screen before editing. Preserve working information architecture, routes, field names, legal copy, and product terminology unless the task explicitly changes them.

## 3. Compose with existing primitives

Start from the product pattern, then map real content and actions into it. Reuse existing tokens and components. Add a semantic token or focused component only when it will represent a stable repeated decision.

Avoid:

- copying an approved sample verbatim when the new task has a different information hierarchy;
- hard-coding repeated visual values inside feature screens;
- replacing native mobile behavior with web-like styling;
- decorative controls with no working state;
- dependency additions for effects achievable with the current stack.

## 4. Implement a complete vertical slice

Include realistic Vietnamese copy and the states required by the workflow. Preserve existing architecture and API boundaries. Keep large style definitions separate from behavior-heavy components when that improves readability.

Treat remote images and API responses as untrusted external inputs. Never place secrets or personal production data in samples.

## 5. Verify the result

Run the repository's own commands. Current baseline commands are:

### Next.js products

```text
npm run format:check
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
```

### Expo product

```text
npm run format:check
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test -- --runInBand
npm run build
```

Then inspect the rendered UI at the intended desktop/mobile viewport and one adjacent breakpoint. Confirm:

- no console/runtime errors;
- no clipped or overflowing Vietnamese text;
- meaningful focus order and accessible names;
- correct image crop and readable overlay contrast;
- visible loading, empty, error, and success behavior where applicable;
- no generated preview files or temporary platform configuration left in the working tree.

For UI changes, save an evidence screenshot in the repository's established output location when one exists. Screenshots support review but do not replace behavioral tests.

Run the product-specific taste pre-flight from `taste-audit.md` against the rendered result. Fix failed checks before delivery; do not waive them merely because automated tests pass.

## 6. Review against five questions

1. Does the screen solve the user's primary task?
2. Does it clearly belong to the correct Wedding product while sharing the brand family?
3. Are hierarchy and states understandable without explanation?
4. Is the implementation accessible, responsive, and maintainable?
5. Did the change avoid copying third-party brand assets and identify temporary photography?

If all five answers are yes and verification passes, proceed without another mockup approval.
````

````text
# Contributing

All four Wedding repositories use `main` as their default integration branch.
Create a short-lived `codex/<module>-<slice>` branch for each change and open a
pull request into `main`.

## Start a change

Run these commands from the repository you are changing:

```powershell
git fetch origin
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch -c codex/my-change
```

Use a descriptive branch name in place of `codex/my-change`. Keep each pull
request focused on one change. For changes spanning repositories, open a pull
request in each affected repository and link the related pull requests.

## Validate and publish

Run the relevant checks in the
[cross-repository development guide](https://github.com/WDP301-wedding/wedding-be/blob/main/docs/cross-repo-development.md#quality-gates).
Commit the reviewed files and push the feature branch:

```powershell
git add <changed-files>
git commit -m "fix: describe the change"
git push -u origin HEAD
```

On GitHub, create a pull request with **base: main** and your feature branch as
the head. Explain the problem, resulting behavior, and validation results.

## Review and merge

Before merging, obtain at least one approval from another team member, resolve
the review conversations, and require all existing CI quality gates to pass.
A failed dependency audit is a failed gate; do not remove or weaken checks to
merge a pull request. New commits require a fresh review.

Merge through the pull request on GitHub. Do not push directly to `main`,
force-push `main`, or delete `main`. When a cross-repository contract pins a
commit SHA, preserve that commit in the merged history or update the consumers
to the final merged artifact before publishing their changes.

After merging, update local `main` with `git pull --ff-only` and start the next
change on a new branch.

## Dependency pull requests

Routine dependency updates run monthly, with at most two npm version-update PRs
and one GitHub Actions version-update PR open per repository. Related React,
Next.js, Prisma, and Vitest packages are grouped where applicable so their
versions are reviewed together. Security updates are not subject to the routine
PR limit; do not close a security update solely to reduce notifications.

The mobile repository limits automated version updates to the committed
manifest ranges. Expo SDK, React, native modules, and Jest upgrades that need
different ranges require a coordinated SDK compatibility review.

An optional version-update PR may be closed or deferred when it does not fix a
current issue, mismatches the approved runtime or SDK, or is superseded by a
reviewed replacement. Closing a PR does not uninstall the existing dependency or
remove project features. Record the reason in the PR when closing it.

## Branch protection availability

The repositories are private. GitHub currently rejects both rulesets and classic
branch protection with HTTP 403 because the current plan does not support this
feature for these repositories. Until protection is enabled, the rules above
are team policy; GitHub does not enforce them against direct pushes.

An organization owner must enable a plan supporting private-repository branch
protection, such as GitHub Team. Then configure `main` to require one approving
review, dismiss stale reviews, require approval of the latest push, resolve all
review conversations, require the existing CI jobs with an up-to-date branch,
apply the rules to administrators, and disallow force pushes and deletion.
````
<!-- CLIENT-SNAPSHOT-END C04 -->

````text
# Wedding Public Web

Next.js application for the public website, Guest invitation/RSVP flows, and Couple web experiences. It consumes the backend contract and never owns database access, privileged credentials, or authoritative business rules.

For the complete four-repository setup and contract workflow, see the backend-owned [cross-repository development guide](https://github.com/WDP301-wedding/wedding-be/blob/main/docs/cross-repo-development.md).

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 24.21.0 (see `.node-version`) and npm 11.x.

```powershell
npm ci
Copy-Item .env.example .env.local
npm run dev -- --port 3000
```

Open `http://localhost:3000`. The default environment points to the backend at `http://localhost:3001`.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` is public browser configuration. Use only a local loopback HTTP URL in development and HTTPS elsewhere. Never place a database URL, service-role key, provider key, bearer token, or other credential in a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable.

## API contract

The generated type declaration at `src/lib/api/generated/schema.d.ts` comes from the backend OpenAPI artifact pinned by exact commit and SHA-256 digest in `api-contract.lock.json`. Keep `wedding-web` and `wedding-be` as sibling directories for the default local source.

```powershell
npm run api:check
npm run api:generate
```

Run `api:check` for normal verification. Run `api:generate` only after the backend contract has been committed and the lock file has been updated to that immutable artifact. Never hand-edit the generated schema.

## Commands

| Command                              | Purpose                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`                        | Start the Next.js development server            |
| `npm run build`                      | Create a production build                       |
| `npm run start`                      | Serve the production build                      |
| `npm run lint`                       | Run ESLint with zero warnings allowed           |
| `npm run typecheck`                  | Generate Next.js types and run TypeScript       |
| `npm run test` / `npm run test:unit` | Run Vitest tests                                |
| `npm run test:coverage`              | Run the coverage gate                           |
| `npm run api:generate`               | Regenerate the typed API schema                 |
| `npm run api:check`                  | Verify the locked artifact and committed schema |
| `npm run format:check`               | Check Prettier formatting                       |

## Troubleshooting

- If browser requests fail, confirm the backend is on port 3001 and includes `http://localhost:3000` in `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`.
- A digest mismatch means the local OpenAPI file is not the artifact recorded in `api-contract.lock.json`; do not bypass it. Update the lock only after the backend contract commit exists.
- Production builds reject a cleartext non-loopback API URL. Use HTTPS outside local development.
````

````text
# Wedding Android App

Expo/React Native Android application for Couple workflows. It consumes the backend contract and never owns database access, privileged credentials, or authoritative business rules.

For the complete four-repository setup and contract workflow, see the backend-owned [cross-repository development guide](https://github.com/WDP301-wedding/wedding-be/blob/main/docs/cross-repo-development.md).

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 24.21.0 (see `.node-version`), npm 11.x, and either an Android emulator or an Android device with Expo Go.

```powershell
npm ci
Copy-Item .env.example .env
npm run android
```

`EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://10.0.2.2:3001` reaches a backend on the host machine from the standard Android emulator. A physical device needs a reachable development-machine address. Use HTTPS outside development.

All `EXPO_PUBLIC_` values are embedded in client output. Never put database credentials, Supabase service-role keys, provider keys, signing material, or EAS access tokens in them. `EXPO_PUBLIC_EAS_PROJECT_ID` remains blank until the Expo project is intentionally linked.

## API contract

The generated type declaration at `src/lib/api/generated/schema.d.ts` comes from the backend OpenAPI artifact pinned by exact commit and SHA-256 digest in `api-contract.lock.json`. Keep `wedding-app` and `wedding-be` as sibling directories for the default local source.

```powershell
npm run api:check
npm run api:generate
```

Run `api:check` for normal verification. Run `api:generate` only after the backend contract has been committed and the lock file has been updated to that immutable artifact. Never hand-edit the generated schema.

## Local Android versus EAS

- `npm run android` starts Expo and opens an Android target for development.
- `npm run build` exports the Android JavaScript bundle to `dist/`; it is the local/CI build gate, not an installable APK.
- `npx eas-cli@23.2.0 build -p android --profile preview` is a manual cloud build. It requires Expo authentication and a linked project, may consume quota or incur cost, and is reserved for the later release stage. CI does not run it.

## Commands

| Command                 | Purpose                                                  |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run start`         | Start the Expo development server                        |
| `npm run android`       | Start Expo and open Android                              |
| `npm run build`         | Export the Android JavaScript bundle locally             |
| `npm run lint`          | Run ESLint with zero warnings allowed                    |
| `npm run typecheck`     | Run TypeScript without emitting files                    |
| `npm run test`          | Run Jest in-band                                         |
| `npm run test:coverage` | Run the Jest coverage gate                               |
| `npm run api:generate`  | Regenerate the typed API schema                          |
| `npm run api:check`     | Verify the locked artifact and committed schema          |
| `npm run audit:ci`      | Run audit-policy tests and the reviewed dependency audit |
| `npm run format:check`  | Check Prettier formatting                                |

## Troubleshooting

- If the emulator cannot reach `localhost`, use `10.0.2.2`; on a physical device, use a reachable LAN address and align backend CORS/network settings.
- A digest mismatch means the local OpenAPI file is not the artifact recorded in `api-contract.lock.json`; do not bypass it. Update the lock only after the backend contract commit exists.
- If EAS asks for login, credentials, or project linking during routine development, stop and use the local Expo commands above.
````
